DAY 2 · WORKSITE ZONES — SEE IT
Access, Hazard and Safe Zones
ACCESS ZONE
The controlled area where rope access is taking place, where
people are at risk of falling: on rope or near a working edge.
HAZARD ZONE
Areas around the Access Zone where people may be at risk
from the work being performed, such as falling objects.
SAFE ZONE
Areas outside the Access and Hazard Zones, safe from the
effects of the rope access work. That does not mean hazard-
free.
THE RULE THE REMINDER
Barricade and sign the Hazard Zone before work starts. The Safe Zone is safe from the rope access work. It is not free of every hazard.

This section defines the requirements for conducting safe and efficient rescue operations during rope

Section 4 — Advanced Rigging
Properly rigging ropes for different situations is critical to safety as a Level 2 technician. Always take
time to consider all of the hazards you are trying to avoid and any new hazards your rigging may
create.
4.1 Rigging Principles — Always Consider
1. Always rig systems that have at least two independent anchors
2. Try to share the load among your anchors — use a Double Figure 8 on a Bight for effective
load distribution
3. Consider the entire rope path when evaluating hazards — not just the anchor point
4. Consider the swing potential when rigging offset anchor systems
4.2 Re-Anchors
Re-anchors are used to get around an obstacle or to avoid a hazard. Before installing a re-anchor,
consider the following:
• Is there sufficient loop length? Insufficient loop makes passing difficult and rescue far more
complex
• Have you actually avoided the hazard? Consider whether rope may contact the structure
during transfer — particularly under platforms
• Do you have ropes leading to the ground on both sides? Install them where convenient —
they are invaluable during rescue
4.3 Deviations
Deviations are used to avoid hazards or reposition ropes. Plan each deviation with the following
questions:
• How great is the angle? Keep the angle at or below 20°. If greater than 20°, rig a re-anchor
instead
• What is the potential for catastrophic failure? If a deviation failure could cause serious harm,
rig a double deviation
• How ergonomic is the deviation for the technician to pass? If difficult, use longer anchor
slings
4.4 Work Restraint Lines (IRATA)
Work restraint lines position a worker near a fall hazard without exposing them to it. Key rigging
requirements:
• Rig lines overhead, as far from the fall hazard as possible
• Ensure the worker's lanyard (cow's tail) is short enough to reach the work area but not long
enough to expose the worker to a fall
• Only one worker may be attached to any single segment of the line at a time

Section 5 — Level 2 Rescue Operations
All Level 2 rescues build on the Level 1 rescue foundation. The key principle in all rescue through
obstacles is to transfer from one rope system to another while the casualty is attached to you.
Regardless of the obstacle — knots, deviations, or re-anchors — the underlying technique remains
consistent.
5.1 Rescue Through Obstacles — Universal Rules
Critical Rules — Apply to ALL Rescue Through Obstacles:
• Ensure the short link connection between you and the casualty is positioned under
all ropes — especially loops. Casualty and rescuer must never be on opposite sides
of a loop
• Go shopping immediately after picking off the casualty — collect the casualty's
descender, a back-up device, and spare carabiners before you need them
• Always use the casualty's cow's tail for the second connection to you — keep your
own cow's tails free for fall factor management during transfers
• Do not tangle cow's tails — check the path of all cow's tails and ropes constantly.
Find hold points and double-check every connection every time
• Always manage your fall factor — consult manufacturer's guidance for the back-up
device in use. Keep back-up device as high as practical at all times
5.2 Rescue from Ascent Mode — Pick-Off from Chest Ascender (IRATA)
This rescue is required for IRATA Level 2. The challenge is lifting the casualty sufficiently to create
slack in the chest ascender so it can be removed. A 4:1 mechanical advantage system is the
recommended method at Sky Tech Academy.
Step-by-Step Procedure
10. Assess the casualty and confirm the rescue can be performed safely — do not proceed if you
put yourself at risk
11. Connect your back-up safety device to the casualty's working rope and your ascenders to the
casualty's safety rope — this allows equal loading of both ropes during ascent
12. Ascend to the casualty until level; place your spare back-up device above the casualty's
ascender and push all the way up; push casualty's hand ascender up too — maintain 4 inch
clearance above toothed devices
13. Remove your first back-up device; ascend past the casualty and change over into your
descender; lock off the descender; clear ropes from between you and the casualty
14. Establish two points of contact: (1) clip casualty's cow's tail into your ventral attachment; (2)
connect short link from your descender carabiner to casualty's sternal attachment — short
link must point downward
15. Confirm two points of contact then remove casualty's hand ascender and back-up device
Sky Tech Academy | Houston, TX | SPRAT & IRATA Certified Training Page 8

Sky Tech Academy | RA Level 2 Binder — SPRAT & IRATA
16. Attach a rope grab above casualty's chest ascender on the working line; add a pulley with
carabiner; using accessory cord, run through casualty's central attachment, through the
pulley, and back twice — creating a 4:1 mechanical advantage system
17. Pull cord to remove all slack between the harness and the pulley/rope grab; add hand
ascender to cord below pulley; shorten foot-loop
18. Keep your back-up device as high as practical; reach down and grasp the casualty at the
waist/ventral attachment; pull up with arms while pushing down with foot — lift casualty
enough to remove chest ascender
19. Apply friction to the mechanical system by squeezing the cord at the bottom of the pulley;
remove hand ascender while holding friction; lower casualty onto the short link; remove lifting
system
20. Add an extra carabiner to your descender carabiner on the side facing you; feed the tail rope
through this carabiner as additional friction; maintain fall factor below 0.5; descend slowly,
keeping the casualty from fully lying on the ground — move legs to restore circulation
⚠ Suspension Trauma: Never allow all weight to be removed from the casualty at once after
prolonged suspension. Sudden pressure release can cause blood to surge through arteries causing
additional injury. Lower slowly and move the casualty's legs continuously to restore circulation.
5.3 Rope to Rope Transfer with Casualty (IRATA)
A relatively straightforward technique. The casualty is already attached to you after a pick-off. There
will be no obstacle in the way during the transfer itself.
21. Pick off casualty; go shopping — collect casualty's descender
22. Add casualty's descender to your harness, capturing your ventral D-ring and the short link
connection; position the descender on the side of your D-ring in the direction of travel
23. Place a safety back-up on the transfer ropes; pull all slack out of the safety line
24. Place the transfer rope into your new descender and remove all slack
25. Install a lifting system: place a rope grab above your descender; run the standing end through
a pulley; attach the pulley to the rope grab — creates a variable ratio lift
26. Place an ascender with foot-loop on the pull rope and climb toward the far anchors
27. Once obstructions are cleared, descend using your original descender to the final destination
5.4 Rescue Through a Small Re-anchor with Casualty (IRATA)
A re-anchor is essentially a series of rope to rope transfers. The casualty will be on the far side of the
re-anchor. Approach using the casualty's safety line as your working line.
28. Pick off the casualty onto your descender carabiner; go shopping; ensure ropes are not under
the short link
29. Descend if above the far anchors — position your descender slightly lower than the far
anchors
30. Add casualty's descender to your harness — capture ventral D-ring and short link; position in
the direction of travel
Sky Tech Academy | Houston, TX | SPRAT & IRATA Certified Training Page 9

Sky Tech Academy | RA Level 2 Binder — SPRAT & IRATA
31. Place a safety back-up on the transfer ropes; pull all slack from safety line without tightening
the cow's tail
32. Place transfer rope into new descender and remove all slack
33. Install a lifting system; climb toward far anchors — do NOT descend into the bottom of the
loop (this creates dangerous loading conditions)
34. Once near far anchors, use original descender to lower until load transfers to new descender;
remove original descender and back-up
35. With exit ropes available, check everything is untangled and not under short link; reposition
original descender to capture both central attachment and short link; add extra back-up to exit
ropes
36. Complete another transfer and descend to the ground
5.5 Rescue Past Knots (SPRAT)
The casualty will be above the knots. Ascend past the casualty, perform a rescue (descent or ascent
mode depending on equipment), go shopping, then descend toward the knots.
37. Ascend past casualty; perform rescue and establish two points of contact; go shopping
(collect descender and back-ups)
38. Descend on working line until the knot below your descender is approximately 60 cm (24
inches) from your descender — allow extra distance for rope stretch on long drops
39. On the safety line, move the existing knot above the height of your descender — take up
slack from above the knot and feed into the bight to isolate the damaged section
40. Add casualty's descender to harness — capture ventral D-ring and short link connection
41. Place a back-up on your working line above your descender (making twins)
42. Feed the rope below the knot in the safety line into the new descender; remove as much
slack as possible
43. Transfer the load from the old descender to the new by operating the old descender (use
additional friction for two-person load)
44. Once transferred, remove the slack descender; remove original back-up; descend down
45. Manage fall factor carefully with two-person load — keep back-up device high at all times
46. Negotiate the knot on your safety line by positioning back-up devices appropriately
5.6 Rescue Past Deviation (IRATA)
Similar in principle to rescue through knots — transferring from the working line to the safety line.
This technique works for both single and double deviations.
47. With casualty attached, descend until the top of your descender is slightly lower than the
lowest deviation anchor connection
48. Using the ropes above the deviation, pull yourself into position at the deviation; grab the
ropes coming from below the deviation; connect them to your harness temporarily
49. Place a back-up above your descender on your working line (making twins)
50. Add casualty's descender to harness — capture ventral D-ring and short link; position on the
side closest to the deviation
Sky Tech Academy | Houston, TX | SPRAT & IRATA Certified Training Page 10

Sky Tech Academy | RA Level 2 Binder — SPRAT & IRATA
51. Install the safety rope (coming from below the deviation) into the new descender; pull all slack
out — move toward the deviation, aiming for approximately 10 cm (4 inches) clearance
52. Lower from old descender to transfer load to safety line below deviation; take off old
descender once slack
53. Manage both back-up devices as you descend — remove first back-up and descend slightly
to position below deviation
54. Add a safety back-up below the deviation; remove the back-up above the deviation; descend
to final destination
5.7 Rescue From Fall Arrest Equipment (IRATA)
Rescuing a casualty who has taken a fall in fall arrest equipment. The quickest approach is rescue
from a separate rope system.
55. Aid climb to the location where the casualty is suspended
56. Install a rope system and attach your descent equipment
57. Descend to the casualty and establish two points of contact as in any other rescue
58. Rig a simple lifting system and lift the casualty, creating slack in their fall arrest lanyard
59. Unclip the fall arrest lanyard from the casualty's harness
60. Lower the casualty onto your short link connection
61. Descend with the casualty to a safe area
5.8 Rescue From an Aid Climb
Rescue from aid climb is particularly challenging because the rescuer is typically at the same level as
or below the casualty, reducing mechanical advantage. A 5:1 mechanical advantage system is
recommended.
62. Aid out to the casualty's location
63. Install a set of ropes at the casualty's location — one rope anchored to the casualty's anchor,
one to your anchor
64. Immediately place the rope at the casualty's anchor into the casualty's descender and
remove all slack; place a safety back-up from the casualty's harness on the rope next to you
— the casualty is now connected to the newly installed ropes
65. Install a 5:1 mechanical advantage lifting system using accessory cord
66. Lift the casualty and release the chest ascender — or alternatively release the carabiner the
cow's tail is connected to the anchor with (if releasing the carabiner, ensure it is on the front
or back of the anchor, never trapped between two loaded carabiners)
67. The casualty is now in descent mode on the ropes you installed — this limits how far you
need to lower them
68. Get onto the opposite ropes and perform a descent rescue
69. Perform a rope to rope transfer with the casualty to reach the final destination if required
5.9 Rescue Hauling — Pitch Head Haul
Sky Tech Academy | Houston, TX | SPRAT & IRATA Certified Training Page 11

Sky Tech Academy | RA Level 2 Binder — SPRAT & IRATA
A pitch head haul system is useful for quickly raising a casualty to a platform, or with modification, to
another accessible area. The rescuer operates from the platform above.
Key Differences from Level 1 Hauling System
70. Do not re-direct ropes through pulleys over the casualty — attach your lowering and lifting
system directly over the casualty instead
71. Use rope grabs to attach your system to the casualty's ropes rather than tying directly to the
load
72. The rope grab on the working line must be a toothed device (e.g. hand ascender) — position
all the way down the working line to the casualty's working equipment
73. The rope grab on the safety line must be a non-aggressive device — position within reach but
with clear separation from the safety back-up
⚠ Load Management: Always pay attention to system loading. Do not make a bad situation worse
by over-stressing a system beyond its Safe Working Load. In complex rescues, consider pre-rigging
and testing the system before the access takes place.
5.10 Cross Haul
A cross haul transports a casualty (or load) horizontally between two anchor systems. The Level 2
may be involved in or required to supervise a team cross haul. Clear roles, planning, and
communication are essential.
Setup
74. Install two haul systems — one anchored over the load, one over the intended landing area
75. Attach the ends of each haul system to the load using a rigging plate — the rigging plate is
essential for multi-directional loading
76. Ensure the rigging plate is backed up along with the rest of the system
Planning Considerations
• What is the included angle at the height of the haul? Greater angle = greater force on each
side of the system
• What is the anticipated total load? Double up on descenders if load is heavy or angles
produce elevated forces
• Are tensions kept equal throughout the system during lowering, especially when load sharing
among anchors?
• How many people are needed to safely operate both systems?
Operation
• Operate one side of the system at a time
• Lift the load first, move to the intended landing area clearing obstacles, then lower using the
other system
• Always keep the load as low as necessary to reduce the included angle
Sky Tech Academy | Houston, TX | SPRAT & IRATA Certified Training Page 12

Sky Tech Academy | RA Level 2 Binder — SPRAT & IRATA
5.11 Tensioned Lines (IRATA)
Tensioned lines distribute forces among many anchors and define the load path. They work in
conjunction with a cross haul system — they do not replace it.
• Install a cross haul first — cross haul systems are the motor behind the operation (lifting,
transporting, and lowering)
• Install tensioned lines at the same level as or above the cross haul, following the same load
path
• Rig tension lines as high as practicable
• Keep the load as low as possible — remember angle loading increases with height
• Do not over-tension lines: maximum tension is one person pulling on a 3:1 mechanical
advantage system — never use more than two people pulling on a 3:1 to tension lines
• Always install at least one control line on the bottom side of a guideline
• During transport, operate the cross haul correctly — use mechanical advantage on the haul
side; put descender(s) into belay mode on the release side
5.12 Vertical Aid Climbing
Vertical aid climb is performed using the same rhythm as horizontal aid climb, adapted for vertical
movement. The same principle applies: maintain two independent points of attachment at all times
with fall factor < 1.

Introduction to Rope Access
Industrial rope access is a safe and efficient method for working at height, allowing technicians to
reach areas that are otherwise difficult or inaccessible. Its effectiveness comes from the strict
application of proven safety principles.
Core Safety Principles
1. Redundant Systems
• Use of a primary working rope alongside an independent backup (safety) rope
• Provides fail-safe fall protection in case one system is compromised
2. Continuous Attachment — 100% Tie-Off
• Technicians are secured at all times while working at height
• Eliminates exposure to unprotected falls
3. Controlled Access and Descent
• Enables precise positioning and movement during work
• Maintains full control during ascent, descent, and task execution
⭐ Key Takeaway: Rope access is one of the safest height-access methods because it is built on
redundancy, constant connection, and controlled movement.

TRAINING DAY 2 Working at Height — Regulations & Fall
Protection
Working at Height — Global Regulatory Overview
Working at height is governed by different regulatory bodies worldwide. While regulations differ by
region, core safety principles remain similar.
Region Governing Body / Standard
United States OSHA — supported by ANSI Z359 standards
United Kingdom HSE — British Standards (BS)
European Union EN Standards
Canada CCOHS — CSA Standards
OSHA & Workplace Safety Overview
What is OSHA?
• OSHA = Occupational Safety and Health Administration
• U.S. authority responsible for developing and enforcing workplace safety laws
• Applies to all workplaces in the United States
OSHA Standards Structure
• 29 CFR 1910 — General Industry
• 29 CFR 1926 — Construction
These are the main regulatory frameworks for workplace safety in the United States.
OSHA vs. ANSI — How They Work Together
OSHA ANSI
Legal authority in the U.S. Develops consensus safety standards
Compliance is mandatory Voluntary by definition
Defines required workplace safety rules Provides detailed technical guidance
Establishes minimum requirements Defines the 'how-to' for compliance
⭐ Key Takeaway: OSHA = What you must follow (law). ANSI = How you safely meet those
requirements. Real compliance requires both working together.
ANSI Z359 Fall Protection Standards

Key Definitions — Fall Protection
Fall Protection
A backup system designed for workers at height when there is a risk of losing balance or falling.
Purpose: to control a fall if it occurs, eliminate or reduce injury risk, and ensure worker safety.
1. Fall Arrest
Designed to safely stop a person already in free fall. Requires a full body harness, energy-absorbing
system, and secure anchor point. Purpose: minimize injury by controlling and stopping the fall.
2. Work Positioning
Supports a worker on a vertical surface (wall, tower, structure) for hands-free work. Uses harness,
ropes, lanyards, and connectors. Purpose: provide stable positioning to perform work safely.
3. Rope Access (Relation to Work Positioning)
Rope access is a form of work positioning system. Technicians are supported by ropes, maintain
hands-free capability, and use controlled movement for access and positioning.
4. Fall Restraint
Prevents the worker from reaching a fall hazard by restricting movement. Purpose: eliminate the
possibility of a fall before it can occur.
5. Managed Fall Arrest Program
A formal employer program to protect employees exposed to fall hazards. Includes procedures,
equipment selection, training, and inspection processes.
⭐ Key Takeaway: Fall Arrest = Protection after a fall starts. Work Positioning = Prevention and
control while working. Rope Access = Advanced work positioning with controlled movement. Fall
Restraint = Prevents access to hazard.
Sky Tech Academy | Houston, TX | SPRAT & IRATA Certified Training Page 7

Sky Tech Academy | Industrial Rope Access Training
Fall Arrest — ANSI Z359.2
Fall arrest systems stop a worker after a fall has occurred, preventing ground contact. The harness
and connecting system absorb energy and safely stop the fall.
Fall Arrest Attachment Points & Force Limits
Connection Point Peak Arrest Force Average Force Max Free-Fall Distance
Sternal (Front) 900 lbs (4 kN) 450 lbs (2 kN) 2 feet
Dorsal (Back) 1,800 lbs (8 kN) 900 lbs (4 kN) 6 feet (unless otherwise
certified)
⭐ Key Takeaway: Sternal = lower forces, shorter falls. Dorsal = higher limits, longer allowable fall
distance. Selection depends on application, system design, and safety requirements.
Work Positioning — ANSI Z359.2
Work positioning systems hold a worker in place while preventing access to fall hazards. The worker
is restrained from reaching an edge — used for support and stability, not fall arrest.
Equipment Requirements
• D-Rings: Minimum Breaking Strength (MBS) = 5,000 lbs (22.2 kN)
• Buckles: Minimum Breaking Strength = 4,000 lbs (17.8 kN)
• Lateral side D-rings must ALWAYS be used in pairs — never individually
• A secondary fall protection system is required when exposure to a fall hazard exists
Work Positioning Anchorage Requirements
• Certified anchorage: must support at least 2× the foreseeable force applied
• Non-certified anchorage: minimum 3,000 lbs (13.3 kN) per worker
• Only one worker may be attached per segment at a time
• Anchor points must be properly positioned to prevent reaching a fall hazard
⭐ Key Takeaway: Work positioning = fall prevention, not fall arrest. Worker must be kept away
from the hazard. A backup system is required if any fall risk exists.
Fall Factor
Fall Factor indicates the severity of a potential fall. It is calculated by dividing the distance of fall by
the length of rope in the system.
Fall Factor = Length of Fall ÷ Length of Rope

FF = 0 0 ft 3 ft ✅ Ideal — no fall
FF = 1 3 ft 3 ft ⚠ Moderate
FF = 2 6 ft 3 ft 🔴🔴 Maximum risk
⭐ Key Takeaway: Keep the backup device as high as practical to minimize fall factor. The goal in
rope access is always FF = 0 or as close as possible.
Fall Protection Saves Lives
Falls from height are one of the leading causes of serious injury and fatalities in the workplace. Most
incidents happen because of incorrect equipment use, poor anchor selection, or lack of inspection or
training.
Fall protection is not optional. Small mistakes at height can have serious or fatal
consequences.

TRAINING DAY 3 Anchor Systems, Load Angles & Load
Limits
Anchor Systems — Critical Safety Principles
Fundamental Rule: No anchor = No safe system
Anchors are the foundation of all rope access work at height. Failure of an anchor results in total
system failure.
Core Requirements
• Anchors must be strong enough for the intended load
• Anchors must be the correct type for the task
• Anchors must be connected to a structurally sound anchorage
System Rules — Non-Negotiable
• Always use TWO independent anchors
• Anchors must be separate and independent
• Failure of one anchor must NOT affect the second
Positioning Rules
• Anchors should be placed to minimize fall distance
• Anchors should reduce swing fall risk
Load Management
• Distribute loads effectively — use load sharing when applicable
• Avoid overloading a single anchor point
Protection & Setup Rules
Anchors must be protected from: sharp edges, heat, abrasion, and chemicals. They must be installed
to prevent movement and avoid accidental disconnection.
⭐ Key Takeaway: Use two independent anchors. Select and position anchors carefully. Protect
and manage loads properly. Safe rope access starts with proper anchor setup and control.
Load Angles — Anchor Angle & Load Distribution
The included angle is the angle between two anchor lines (rope-to-rope), measured on the inside of
the system. As the included angle increases, force on each anchor increases and load sharing
becomes less efficient.

MODULE 1 — Introduction to Rope Access
1.1 What Is Rope Access?
Rope access is an industrial work method that uses techniques adapted from caving and rock
climbing to move up, down, or across ropes to reach elevated or difficult-to-access locations. It is
widely recognized as one of the safest and most efficient methods for working at height.
At Sky Tech Academy, students will learn that rope access is not simply a climbing skill — it is a
structured, regulated profession built on a foundation of safety, redundancy, and technical
competence.
Key Principles of Rope Access
• Origin from caving and rock climbing techniques, adapted for industrial use
• Considered safer than many traditional access methods such as scaffolding
• Always uses two independent rope systems simultaneously:
◦ Working rope (main line) — primary load-bearing system
◦ Safety rope (backup line) — independent secondary protection
• All critical components are backed up — anchors, ropes, and attachment points
• Uses front (ventral) attachment points for better control and positioning
• Specialized lightweight equipment designed specifically for industrial operations
• Workers remain continuously supported — known as the 'post-fall' working position
• Fast and efficient — significantly reduces mobilization time vs. scaffolding
⭐ Key Highlight: Industrial Rope Access is a safe, efficient, and highly controlled method of
working at height using dual-rope systems and specialized training.
1.2 Rope Access vs. Scaffolding
Comparison Factor Rope Access Scaffolding
Flexibility Flexible and mobile — adapts to Fixed structure — limited to
complex structures planned access points

dismantling

hazards specific risks

certification (SPRAT/IRATA) with minimal training

Rope Access Training Curriculum | Sky Tech Academy

1.3 Safety Advantages of Rope Access
When a fall occurs using a conventional fall arrest system (such as scaffolding with dorsal D-ring
attachment), the worker is suspended between the shoulder blades. This position can be
uncomfortable, unstable, and may make self-rescue difficult. Prolonged suspension in this position
can lead to suspension trauma (orthostatic intolerance), which may become life-threatening within
approximately 20 minutes if rescue is not performed.
Rope access systems are fundamentally different. The dual-rope system means technicians are
always connected to two independent lines, dramatically reducing the risk of a fall occurring at all.
Key safety features include:
• Dual protection — working line and safety backup line at all times
• Reduced shock loading — workers are pre-supported, not falling
• Lower fall factor — backup device positioned as high as practical
• Controlled working position — stable, hands-free operation
• Smaller teams — fewer personnel exposed to risk
⭐ Key Highlight: Rope access safety is built on redundancy and controlled fall risk — dual
independent systems prevent failure while fall factor management minimizes consequences of any
potential fall.
1.4 Cost Efficiency
Beyond safety, rope access delivers significant financial benefits. A study conducted at an industrial
refinery comparing traditional scaffolding with rope access for the same scope of work found that
rope access reduced overall project costs by approximately 62%. This savings comes from reduced
material costs, smaller teams, faster mobilization, and lower overall exposure hours.
1.5 Rope Access as an Access Method — Not the Work Itself
A critical concept for all Sky Tech Academy students: rope access is a method of reaching the
worksite — it is not the work itself. Technicians will receive additional training specific to their trade or
assigned tasks, which may include:
• Inspection and Non-Destructive Testing (NDT)
• Maintenance and mechanical work
• Installation and construction tasks

Rope Access Training Curriculum | Sky Tech Academy
• Painting, coating, and surface preparation
• Other specialized industrial services
⭐ Key Highlight: Rope access provides safe access — professional competence comes from
combining rope access skills with your trade or technical discipline.

MODULE 2 — Fall Protection Principles & Regulations
2.1 Fall Protection Overview
Fall protection refers to the systems and measures used to keep workers safe while working at
height, either by preventing a fall from occurring or safely arresting a fall if it does occur. Fall
protection programs are established and enforced by the employer, who is responsible for ensuring a
safe working environment.
2.2 The Three Types of Fall Protection Systems
TYPE 1 — Fall Arrest
Designed to stop a worker after a fall has already occurred. Typically involves a full body harness,
lanyard or SRL, and anchorage point. Fall arrest is considered less effective than prevention
because some force is still transferred to the body.
TYPE 2 — Fall Restraint / Travel Restraint
Prevents the worker from reaching a fall hazard in the first place by restricting movement. A properly
adjusted lanyard on a horizontal lifeline, for example, allows movement within a safe zone but
prevents reaching the edge. This method effectively eliminates fall risk.
TYPE 3 — Work Positioning
Supports part or all of the worker's weight through ropes and associated equipment. Widely used in
rope access, this system allows the technician to maintain a stable, hands-free working position on
structures such as walls, towers, and vertical surfaces.
2.3 Fall Factor
Fall Factor indicates the severity of a potential fall. It is calculated by dividing the maximum distance
a worker could fall by the total length of the rope or connection between the worker and the anchor
point. A higher fall factor represents a more severe fall and increased stress on the system.
Backup Position Fall Distance Rope Length Fall Factor
Backup high (as practical) 0 ft 3 ft FF = 0 (Ideal)
Backup at attachment level 3 ft 3 ft FF = 1
Backup very low (by feet) 6 ft 3 ft FF = 2 (Maximum
risk)

2.7 Regulatory Framework — OSHA & ANSI
In the United States, fall protection is governed by OSHA (Occupational Safety and Health
Administration) under two primary standards:
• 29 CFR 1910 — General Industry
• 29 CFR 1926 — Construction
ANSI (American National Standards Institute) develops voluntary performance and testing standards
for fall protection equipment. However, when OSHA adopts ANSI standards into its regulations,
compliance becomes mandatory.
Key ANSI Z359 standards relevant to rope access:

130–310 lbs)

(SRLs) alongside rope access systems
⭐ Key Highlight: OSHA requires employers to implement structured fall protection programs
aligned with ANSI standards, ensuring workers are protected through compliant equipment,
procedures, and safe practices.
2.8 Self-Retracting Lifelines (SRLs)
SRLs are designed to rapidly arrest a fall while minimizing free-fall distance. They use an internal
inertial braking mechanism that activates when sudden acceleration is detected. Key considerations
when using SRLs:
• Choose the correct attachment point (sternal or dorsal) based on device specifications
• Dorsal connection may result in forward-leaning fall — risk of impact with adjacent structures
such as ladders
• Sternal attachment must be confirmed compatible with device force ratings
• Twin SRLs provide 100% tie-off but add weight and bulk
• Always inspect before use — verify force ratings and compatibility with work conditions

understanding of how the device behaves in real fall scenarios.

MODULE 3 — SPRAT Standards & Certification
3.1 What Is SPRAT?
The Society of Professional Rope Access Technicians (SPRAT) is the primary governing body for
rope access work in North America. SPRAT provides a structured framework for training,
certification, and safe work practices, and its certifications are widely required by industrial employers
across the United States.

3.3 SPRAT Certification Levels
LEVEL 1 — Rope Access Technician — Entry Level

MODULE 4 — IRATA Standards & Certification
4.1 What Is IRATA?
The Industrial Rope Access Trade Association (IRATA) is the internationally recognized standard for
rope access, widely used in offshore oil & gas, construction, and energy sectors globally. IRATA has
been established longer than SPRAT, reflecting the earlier adoption of rope access techniques in
Europe. While both organizations share similar safety goals, IRATA documentation is significantly
more detailed and comprehensive.
4.2 International Code of Practice (ICOP)
IRATA's primary document is the International Code of Practice (ICOP), divided into four parts:
ICOP Part Title Content Summary
Part 1 General Information Introduction, scope, terminology, and basic principles of
rope access. Defines key elements of a safe system of
work.
Part 2 Detailed Guidance In-depth guidance on planning, personnel selection,
equipment requirements, and practical work methods
from start to finish.
Part 3 Informative Annexes Risk assessment, equipment inspection, anchor systems,
suspension trauma, rope access techniques, and
environmental factors.
Part 4 Local Legislation Region-specific legal requirements (primarily UK).
Provides useful regulatory insight.
4.3 IRATA Key Safety Principles (ICOP Part 1)
• Proper planning and effective management of all operations
• Use of trained and competent personnel at all times
• Adequate supervision — only a Level 3 can act as safety supervisor
• Careful selection of suitable equipment for the task
• Proper inspection, maintenance, and traceability of all equipment
• Maximum impact force on a falling technician limited to 6 kN (~1,348 lbf)
• Mandatory exclusion zones — anchor area, working edge, intermediate level, and bottom
level
• Documented and communicated rescue procedures before work begins
• Continuous improvement through internal and IRATA audits

MODULE 5 — Roles & Responsibilities
5.1 Employer Responsibilities
Under both SPRAT and IRATA, the employer bears primary responsibility for establishing and

5.2 Rope Access Program Administrator

The Program Administrator is responsible for:

MECHANICAL ADVANTAGE initially seem complex. However, by breaking the concept into simple components, it becomes much easier to
grasp.
1. Fixed Pulleys
In this section, we will explore how adding specific equipment to rope systems can reduce the effort required
2. Moving Pulleys to lift a load. The primary tools used for this purpose are pulleys and rope-grabbing devices. These
components either redirect the rope (as in a fixed pulley) or distribute the load in a way that makes it easier to
3. Purpose of Mechanical Advantage
raise (as in a movable pulley).
4. Rope Grabs When we refer to mechanical advantage, we are simply describing any setup connected to a load that reduces
5. Compound and Complex Systems the amount of force needed to lift it. In short, it is a method of making work more efficient by using equipment
strategically.
6. Piggyback Systems
7. Z-Rig System Throughout this section, different pulley systems will be explained to help you understand how mechanical
advantage works in practice. Learners at more advanced levels (Level 2 and Level 3) are encouraged to review
all systems discussed, while Level 1 learners may focus on the fundamental concepts introduced at the
beginning.
To begin, consider a load weighing approximately 100 kg (about 220 pounds), which represents the weight of
an average worker.

If we attempt to lift a load directly by hand, we must apply a force equal to its weight. For example, lifting a 100 kg (220
lb) load requires approximately the same amount of effort. In practical terms, this is difficult for most individuals to
achieve safely.
Attaching the load to a rope does not change this requirement. If the rope is pulled upward, the same amount of force is
still needed to raise the load. While the method changes slightly, the effort required remains unchanged.
To improve efficiency, we can introduce a pulley positioned above the load, often referred to as the anchor point or pitch
head. This is the location where the rope system is secured before running down to the load. By routing the rope through
a pulley at this point, the direction of force is changed - allowing us to pull downward instead of lifting upward.
Although this setup makes the task more practical and ergonomically efficient, it does not reduce the force required. A
fixed pulley does not create mechanical advantage; it simply redirects the rope to a more favorable working position.
It is also important to recognize that the anchor system must be capable of supporting the full load. All hardware used -
including pulleys, carabiners, and connectors - must be properly rated and suitable for the expected forces.
A key principle to understand is that a fixed (non-moving) pulley does not make lifting easier in terms of effort. Its role
is limited to redirecting the rope, which can improve handling and operator efficiency.
Another important factor in rope systems is friction. Every component added - such as pulleys and carabiners -
introduces some resistance, which reduces overall system efficiency. For learning purposes, systems are often described
as if they operate without friction (100% efficiency). However, in real-world conditions, this is never the case.
Pulleys are designed to minimize friction and are rated based on their efficiency. High-quality pulleys typically operate
at around 90% efficiency or higher. The closer a pulley is to 100% efficiency, the less energy is lost due to friction,
resulting in a more effective system.

If we adjust the setup and attach the pulley directly to the load instead of the anchor point, the pulley will move as the load is raised. This change is important
because once the pulley moves with the load, the system begins to create mechanical advantage.
Only moving pulleys reduce the amount of force required by the operator. This is the key principle behind mechanical advantage—using equipment to reduce effort
while still accomplishing the same task.
Understanding Mechanical Advantage
Mechanical advantage describes how effectively a system multiplies the force applied by the user. In simple terms, it allows a smaller input force to move a larger
load.
From a theoretical standpoint, mechanical advantage is expressed as the ratio between the output force (the force lifting the load) and the input force (the effort
applied). These calculations often assume an ideal, friction-free system. However, in real-world conditions, friction is always present.
Because of this, the actual mechanical advantage is always lower than the theoretical value. Factors such as pulley efficiency, rope condition, and additional
hardware all contribute to energy loss within the system. Even high-quality pulleys, which may operate at around 90% efficiency, still introduce some resistance.
A Simpler Way to View It
Mechanical advantage can be understood more practically as a way to:
• Increase the effective force applied to a system
• Reduce the effort required to lift or move a load
When you pull on a rope within a mechanical system, your applied force is distributed and multiplied through the setup. However, friction reduces the total
effectiveness, meaning more effort is required than theoretical calculations might suggest.
Key Takeaways
Mechanical advantage is created whenever a moving pulley is introduced into the system.
Fixed pulleys do not create mechanical advantage—they only redirect the rope.
All systems experience some loss of efficiency due to friction.
Mechanical advantage systems are generally categorized into three types:
Simple systems
Compound systems
Complex systems
Each of these system types will be explored in the following sections, with practical examples to demonstrate their use and application in the field.

Simple Mechanical Advantage Systems
In this section, we will simplify our calculations by assuming an ideal system with 100% efficiency, meaning friction and energy loss are not
considered. While real-world systems always involve some friction, this approach makes it easier to understand the core principles.
A simple mechanical advantage system is created when one or more moving pulleys are directly attached to the load. These systems reduce the
amount of effort needed to lift the load by distributing the force across multiple rope segments.
Example: 2:1 Mechanical Advantage
Consider a setup where a single moving pulley is attached to the load. In this configuration, the effort required to lift the load is effectively reduced
by half. This is known as a 2:1 mechanical advantage system, meaning the input force is doubled within the system.
The reason for this is straightforward: two sections of rope are supporting the load. Each section shares part of the weight, reducing the effort
needed by the operator.
Adding a Fixed Pulley
If we add a pulley at the anchor point (often referred to as the pitch head) to make pulling more convenient, the system does not gain additional
mechanical advantage. This is because the pulley remains stationary.
A fixed pulley only changes the direction of the pull, allowing the operator to pull down instead of lifting upward. While this can improve
efficiency from a handling standpoint, it does not reduce the force required.
Determining Mechanical Advantage: The “Counting Lines” Method
A simple way to identify mechanical advantage is to use the counting lines method:
• Count the number of rope segments directly supporting the load
• Do not include the rope segment you are pulling if it passes through a fixed pulley
For example:
• If two rope segments support the load, the system provides a 2:1 mechanical advantage
• The applied effort line is excluded if it only redirects through a non-moving pulley
This method provides a quick and reliable way to evaluate simple systems in the field.

Expanding the System
If we introduce an additional pulley into the system (such as using a double pulley or multiple pulleys at the anchor and load), we can further increase the
mechanical advantage, In practice:
• The anchor (pitch head) typically holds one or more fixed pulleys
• The load is connected to one or more moving pulleys
As more moving pulleys are added, the mechanical advantage increases, reducing the effort required. However, this also adds complexity to the system and requires
careful setup and inspection.
Expanding Simple Mechanical Advantage Systems
Using the counting lines method, we can determine that this configuration provides a 4:1 mechanical advantage. In an ideal system, this means the effort required
to lift the load is reduced to approximately 25% of the load’s weight.
It is important to note that the fixed pulleys in this setup do not contribute to mechanical advantage. Their primary function is to redirect the rope and, in some
cases, help distribute forces across anchor points. However, if multiple pulleys are connected to the same anchor, all resulting forces are still applied to that single
anchor. This highlights the importance of ensuring that anchor systems are properly rated and secure.
Recognizing Mechanical Advantage Patterns
As systems become more advanced, clear patterns begin to emerge:
• When the anchor is positioned at the pitch head (top), the mechanical advantage typically follows an even-number ratio (e.g., 2:1, 4:1, 6:1).
• When the anchor is attached to the load, the system produces an odd-number ratio (e.g., 3:1, 5:1).
Understanding this pattern helps in quickly estimating system performance during setup and operation.
Example Configurations
• A system configured with the anchor at the load and a single moving pulley can produce a 3:1 mechanical advantage.
• Adding a pulley at the anchor (pitch head) in this case will only change the direction of pull—it does not increase mechanical advantage.
• By adding another moving pulley to the load, along with a pulley at the anchor for rope routing, the system can be increased to a 5:1 mechanical advantage.
These examples demonstrate how increasing the number of moving pulleys directly affects the system’s efficiency, while fixed pulleys mainly improve usability and
rope direction.
Key Considerations
Mechanical advantage depends on the number of rope segments supporting the load.
Fixed pulleys assist with rope direction but do not reduce effort.
All forces in the system must be carefully evaluated, especially at anchor points.
As mechanical advantage increases, system complexity also increases, requiring greater attention to setup and safety.

Compound Mechanical Advantage Systems
A simple mechanical advantage system is created when all moving pulleys are attached directly to the load. In contrast, a compound mechanical advantage system is formed when one simple
system is used to pull another. In these systems, all moving pulleys typically travel in the same direction, working together to further reduce the effort required.
System Overview
To build a compound system, we can begin with a basic 2:1 mechanical advantage setup. Instead of holding the rope manually, a rope-grabbing device is added to the system to capture and hold
progress. This allows the operator to reset their position on the rope without losing any gained distance.
Rope grabs are devices designed to hold the rope securely under load and prevent it from slipping. Common examples include handled ascenders, cam-based devices, and friction-based rope
grabs. These tools are essential for maintaining control and efficiency in hauling systems.
The rope is then routed through a fixed pulley at the anchor point (pitch head). This allows the operator to pull in a downward direction, improving ergonomics and control without adding
mechanical advantage.
Next, the rope is passed through an additional pulley that is attached to the rope grab. At this stage, the system becomes a compound configuration, combining two simple systems:
• A 2:1 system acting on the load
• A 3:1 system (commonly known as a Z-rig) pulling on the first system
The Z-Rig
The 3:1 mechanical advantage system, often called a Z-rig, is one of the most widely used hauling systems in rope operations. It is valued for its balance between simplicity, efficiency, and
effectiveness.
In a compound arrangement, the Z-rig plays a critical role by amplifying the applied force and making it possible to move heavier loads with less effort. Because of its reliability and relatively
straightforward setup, it is frequently used in lifting, hauling, and rescue scenarios.
Key Takeaways
• Compound systems are created by combining multiple simple mechanical advantage systems
• A rope grab allows progress capture and hands-free operation
• Fixed pulleys improve direction of pull but do not increase mechanical advantage
• The Z-rig (3:1 system) is a fundamental and widely used component in compound systems

Understanding Forces in a Compound System
Let’s examine how forces are applied within a compound mechanical advantage system.
• The first part of the system is a 2:1 mechanical advantage setup.
• The second part is a 3:1 mechanical advantage system, commonly referred to as a Z-rig.
Step-by-Step Force Analysis
In the 2:1 system, a 100 kg load is supported by two rope segments. This reduces the required effort to:
100 kg÷2=50 kg100{kg}
This means the rope grab - connected to the 2:1 system - is effectively pulling on a 50 kg load.
Next, the 3:1 system (Z-rig) is used to pull that 50 kg force. Applying the same principle:
50 kg÷3=16.7 kg (approximately)
So, the operator only needs to apply about 16.7 kg of force to move the original 100 kg load (in an ideal, friction-free system).
Total Mechanical Advantage
A simpler way to evaluate compound systems is to calculate the total mechanical advantage (MA) by multiplying the individual systems:
Total MA=MA1×MA2
In this example:
2:1×3:1=6:1
This means the entire system provides a 6:1 mechanical advantage.
General Formula
To calculate the required effort in any system, use the formula:
Force Required=LoadMechanical Advantage Add your body text
Applying it here:
100 kg:6≈16.7 kg
Key Takeaways
• Compound systems combine multiple simple mechanical advantage systems
• The total mechanical advantage is found by multiplying each system’s ratio
• A 2:1 system feeding into a 3:1 system results in a 6:1 system
• As mechanical advantage increases, the required input force decreases
• In real-world conditions, friction will increase the actual effort required
This example demonstrates how compound systems significantly reduce the force needed to move heavy loads, making them highly effective in lifting and hauling operations.

Practical Considerations of Compound Mechanical Advantage Systems
In rope access, rescue, and rigging operations, compound mechanical advantage systems are commonly used during planning, setup, and execution. These systems are often preferred because
they can achieve higher mechanical advantage with less rope compared to equivalent simple systems, and they tend to operate more efficiently overall.
However, these benefits come with certain trade-offs.
Complexity and Efficiency
Compound systems are inherently more complex than simple mechanical advantage systems. This increased complexity can make them more challenging to set up correctly, especially for less
experienced users. If not assembled properly, the system may:
• Introduce unnecessary friction
• Operate less efficiently than intended
• Fail to deliver the expected mechanical advantage
For this reason, careful attention to rigging technique and system layout is essential.
Rope Travel and System Movement
Another important factor to consider is rope travel distance. As mechanical advantage increases, the amount of rope that must be pulled also increases.
A simple guideline is:
• A 5:1 system requires approximately 5 times the rope travel to move the load a given distance
In practical terms, this means:
• Lifting a load becomes easier in terms of force
• However, it takes more time and effort in terms of rope handling
• Progress capture devices (such as rope grabs) will need to be reset periodically as the system advances
Key Takeaways
• Compound systems are widely used due to their efficiency and reduced rope requirements
• Increased mechanical advantage reduces effort but increases system complexity
• Higher ratios require more rope movement to achieve the same lifting distance
• Proper setup and monitoring are critical to ensure safe and effective operation
Understanding these trade-offs allows operators to choose the most appropriate system for the task, balancing efficiency, simplicity, and safety.

The “T-Method” (Tension Method)
The first key concept to understand when using the T-Method is:
• When force is applied to one side of a pulley, an equal force exists on the other side of that pulley (assuming an ideal system without friction).
What Is the T-Method?
The T-Method (Tension Method) is a systematic approach used to calculate mechanical advantage by tracking tension forces throughout a rope system. Instead of only counting rope segments, this
method provides a deeper understanding of how forces are distributed across the system.
Steps for Applying the T-Method
• Divide the System
Break down the overall system into individual simple mechanical advantage systems.
• Start at the Haul Line
Begin at the input (haul line) and assign a tension value to the rope. This is typically your starting force.
• Track Tensions Through the First System
Follow the rope through each pulley and note how many tensioned rope segments are present. Each segment carries the same level of tension in an ideal system.
• Evaluate Connection Points
At pulleys or rope grabs connecting one system to another, add together the tensions acting there. This total force becomes the input for the next part of the system.
• Apply Tension to the Next System
Use the calculated force from the previous step as the input force for the next simple mechanical advantage system.
• Repeat the Process
Continue working through each section of the system, calculating and transferring tension values step by step.
• Determine Mechanical Advantage at the Load
Once all tensions are identified, count the total number of tensioned rope segments supporting the load. This total represents the mechanical advantage of the system.
Important Notes
• Although the final mechanical advantage is determined at the load, you must evaluate every tension throughout the system to understand how forces are applied.
• The analysis should begin from the input (haul side) and progress toward the load.
• In real-world applications, friction will reduce efficiency, so the calculated values represent ideal conditions.
Key Takeaways
The T-Method provides a structured way to analyze complex systems
It is based on understanding how tension is shared and transferred
Equal tension exists on both sides of a pulley in ideal conditions
Complex systems are easier to evaluate when broken into smaller, simple systems
Accurate analysis improves both efficiency and safety in rigging operations

Applying the T-Method to Mechanical Advantage Systems
Let’s begin by applying the T-Method to a simple mechanical advantage system.
Example: Simple System
In this example, the rope segments are labeled A, B, and C.
• Starting at the haul line (A), when force is applied, it carries one unit of tension.
• Because tension is equal on both sides of a pulley (in an ideal system), the next rope segment (B) also carries one unit of tension.
• At the redirect pulley, these tensions combine, meaning the pulley experiences two units of tension.
Continuing through the system:
• Rope (C) will also carry one unit of tension, as it is part of the same continuous system.
• At the pulley attached to the load, the tensions from ropes (B) and (C) combine.
This results in two tensioned rope segments supporting the load, giving a 2:1 mechanical advantage.
Example: Compound System
Now let’s apply the same method to a compound mechanical advantage system.
Step 1: Break the System into Parts
The overall system is divided into two simpler systems:
• A 3:1 mechanical advantage system (outer system)
• A 2:1 mechanical advantage system connected to the load
Step 2: Analyze the First System (3:1)
The outer system operates as a standard 3:1 setup. At the end of this system, a rope grab is used to capture progress.
In this context, the rope grab acts as the load for the 3:1 system. The tensions generated here will be transferred into the next system.
Step 3: Analyze the Second System (2:1)
The rope grab from the first system now applies force to the 2:1 system, which is directly connected to the load.
Step 4: Combine the Results
The tensions produced by the 3:1 system become the input force for the 2:1 system. By tracking how tension moves through both systems.
Key Takeaways
• Always break complex systems into simple components before analyzing
• Track tension step by step through each rope and pulley
• A rope grab can act as a transfer point for force between systems
The final mechanical advantage is determined by the total tensions acting on the load
Using the T-Method in this structured way allows for accurate analysis of both simple and compound systems, improving understanding, efficiency, and safety in rigging operations.

Applying the T-Method to a Compound System (Step-by-Step)
In this example, the compound mechanical advantage system consists of two simple systems:
• A 3:1 mechanical advantage system (outer system)
• A 2:1 mechanical advantage system connected to the load
Step 2: Start with the Outermost System
Begin by analyzing the outermost simple system, which in this case is the 3:1 mechanical advantage system.
Step 3: Assign Tension Values
As force is applied to the haul line:
• The input rope carries one unit of tension
• Because tension is equal on both sides of a pulley, the rope on the opposite side of the first pulley also carries one unit of tension
Since the first pulley is attached to the load (moving pulley), it creates mechanical advantage.
The rope then continues through the next pulley and connects to the rope grab.
Now, evaluate the forces on each component:
• Each pulley has one unit of tension on each side, resulting in two tensions acting on each pulley
• The rope grab is connected to the moving part of the system, so it also experiences two units of tension
Step 4: Transfer Tension to the Next System
To determine the force applied to the next system:
• Add the tension in the rope connected to the rope grab (1 unit)
• Add the tension acting on the rope grab itself (2 units)
1+2=3
This means the rope grab applies three units of tension to the next system.
Step 5: Apply Force to the Second System
The calculated 3 units of tension now become the input force for the second simple mechanical advantage system (the 2:1 system connected to the load).
By continuing this process through the remaining system, you can determine the total mechanical advantage and understand exactly how force is distributed.
Key Takeaways
• Always begin analysis with the outermost system
• Assign one unit of tension to the haul line and track it through the system
• Moving pulleys multiply force, while rope grabs transfer force between systems
• Add tensions at connection points to determine input for the next system
• Continue step-by-step until reaching the load
This structured approach ensures accurate evaluation of even complex rigging systems, improving both performance and safety in practical applications.

Completing the T-Method and Introducing Complex Systems
Step 6: Continue the Process
Following Step 6 of the T-Method, we repeat the same process for the next stage of the system.
If 3 units of tension are applied to the hauling rope, then—based on the principle of equal tension across a pulley—the opposite side of the pulley will also carry 3 units of tension.
These forces combine at the pulley attached directly to the load:
3+3=6 units of tension
Since this pulley is the only component connected to the load, we can conclude that the system applies 6 units of tension to lift a single load, resulting in a 6:1 mechanical advantage.
Transition to Complex Mechanical Advantage Systems
Up to this point, we have examined:
• Simple mechanical advantage systems
• Compound mechanical advantage systems
We will now move on to complex mechanical advantage systems.
What Defines a Complex System?
A system is considered complex when:
• One or more pulleys move in a different or opposite direction compared to the rest of the system, or
• The direction of movement within the system differs from the direction of the load
This variation in motion introduces additional complexity and requires a more detailed analysis.
Example: Building a Complex System
To form a complex system, we can expand a compound system by adding another simple mechanical advantage system.
In this configuration:
• The system contains three individual simple mechanical advantage systems
• The outermost system operates in the opposite direction of the other two
• This opposing movement is what classifies the system as complex
Applying the T-Method to a Complex System
Step 2 – Assign Initial Tension
Start with the outermost system and apply one unit of tension to the haul line.

Step 3 – Evaluate Each Device
Track the tension through all ropes and components within that system (up to the next rope grab).
• Add the tensions on both sides of each pulley
• Apply the total to each device
In this example:
• The outer system contains two pulleys and one rope grab
• The second system contains one pulley and one rope grab
• The third system contains one pulley connected to the load
Step 4 – Combine Tensions at Rope Grabs
At each rope grab, add:
• The tension in the incoming rope
• The tension acting on the rope grab
This produces the force transferred to the next system.
Step 5 – Transfer Force
Apply the calculated force to the haul line of the next mechanical advantage system.
Step 6 – Repeat
Continue this process through all systems until every rope and component has been assigned a tension value.
Step 7 – Determine Mechanical Advantage
Add together the tension values acting on all components directly connected to the load.
Final Result
In this example, the total number of tensions acting on the load equals 10 units, resulting in a:
10:1 mechanical advantage
Key Takeaways
Complex systems involve multiple simple systems working in different directions
The T-Method remains the most effective way to analyze these systems
Always work step-by-step, transferring tension through each stage

System Forces
Now that you understand how to build mechanical advantage systems and calculate their ratios, it is important to examine how these systems affect forces acting on
equipment and anchors.
Calculating Forces in a System
The process for determining forces is straightforward:
Step 1 – Identify Mechanical Advantage
Determine the total mechanical advantage (MA) of the system.
Step 2 – Calculate Force per Tension Unit
Divide the load by the mechanical advantage:
Force per unit=Load:Mechanical Advantage
Step 3 – Apply to Each Component
Multiply the force per unit by the number of tensioned rope segments acting on each component.
Example: 6:1 Mechanical Advantage System
For a 100 kg load with a 6:1 mechanical advantage:
100÷6≈16.7 kg
• A pulley with 2 tensioned rope segments:
2×16.7=33.4 kg
• A pulley connected directly to the load with 6 tension units:
6×16.7≈100 kg6
This confirms that the system correctly supports the full load.
These same forces are transferred through connected components, including rope grabs and redirect pulleys.
Understanding Anchor Loads
Anchor forces must also be carefully evaluated. 1.
In this example:
• The load is distributed across the system
• The anchor supports approximately 50 kg
• The hauling side also carries part of the load
At first glance, the redirect pulley may appear to carry less force (~33.4 kg). However, the haul line itself contributes additional force (~16.7 kg). When combined, the
total force balance remains consistent.

Complex Systems and Force Distribution
In complex mechanical advantage systems, force distribution can become less intuitive.
For example:
• One anchor may carry 50 kg
• Another part of the system may carry 60 kg
This occurs because force is redistributed differently when pulleys move in opposing directions. As a result, some anchors can experience higher-than-expected loads.
This is a critical consideration when designing rigging systems. Using methods such as the T-Method helps identify and account for these forces in advance.
Practical Considerations
• Friction Is Always Present
No system operates at 100% efficiency. Every contact point introduces friction and reduces overall performance.
• Pulleys Improve Efficiency
High-quality pulleys are typically over 90% efficient, with some reaching 94–98% efficiency, making them essential for reducing energy loss.
• Carabiners Increase Friction
Carabiners can significantly increase resistance and should be minimized in hauling systems where efficiency matters.
• Higher MA = More Rope Travel
Increasing mechanical advantage reduces effort but requires more rope movement and frequent resetting of progress capture devices.
• Use Only What You Need
Select a system with sufficient mechanical advantage, but avoid unnecessary complexity.
Final Notes
Mechanical advantage systems are powerful tools for safely and efficiently moving loads. While this section provides a strong foundation, there is always more to learn and
refine through experience.
Remember:
• Rope access is a means to perform work, not the work itself
• Efficient systems reduce fatigue and improve safety
• Proper planning and understanding of forces are essential
Even a simple component like a pulley can dramatically improve performance when used correctly. With practice, these systems become easier to understand and apply
effectively in real-world situations.

Rope Protection
Care shall be taken to ensure that ropes are protected from hazards commonly found at the worksite. These hazards include sharp edges, abrasive surfaces, corrosive substances, and
heat sources. Whenever possible, such hazards should be completely removed from the worksite.
If removal is not feasible, ropes must be rigged in a way that avoids contact with these hazards. As a final precaution, appropriate rope protectors should be installed to reduce the
impact of the hazard to an acceptable level.
Personnel must demonstrate an awareness of the potential consequences of hazards affecting equipment, as well as the methods for removing, avoiding, containing, or
reducing these hazards. They must also understand how movement (such as rope motion, load shifts, or environmental changes) may increase the risk posed by these hazards.

Rope Access Level 1 Technician
Rope access training at Level 1 is structured around two essential components: theoretical knowledge and practical
demonstration. Candidates are first required to understand the technical principles that form the foundation of safe
rope access operations. This knowledge is assessed through a written examination and includes an understanding of
equipment, safety factors, and general working principles. However, theoretical understanding alone is not sufficient;
it must be supported by the ability to apply these concepts in real situations.

• Double Figure of Eight
4. Use of the Work Seat (IRATA)
• Figure of Nine
5. Passing Knots • Joining knot

Introduction to Rope Access
Industrial rope access is a safe and efficient method for working at height, allowing technicians to reach
areas that are otherwise difficult or inaccessible. Its effectiveness comes from the strict application of proven
safety principles.
Core Safety Principles
1. Redundant Systems
• Use of a primary working rope alongside an independent backup (safety) rope
• Provides fail-safe fall protection in case one system is compromised
2. Continuous Attachment (100% Tie-Off)
• Technicians are secured at all times while working at height
• Eliminates exposure to unprotected falls
3. Controlled Access and Descent
• Enables precise positioning and movement during work
• Maintains full control during ascent, descent, and task execution
Key Takeaway
Rope access is considered one of the safest height-access methods because it is built on:
• Redundancy – Backup systems prevent single-point failure
• Constant connection – Workers are always secured
• Controlled movement – Ensures stability and precision
When properly implemented, these principles make rope access a highly reliable and low-risk solution for working
at height.

Working at Height Rules
Global Regulatory Overview
Working at height is governed by different regulatory bodies worldwide, each with its own standards and requirements:
• United States: OSHA (supported by ANSI Z359 standards)
• United Kingdom: HSE (British Standards – BS)
• European Union: EN Standards
• Canada: CCOHS (CSA Standards)
While regulations differ by region, core safety principles remain similar, though specific requirements, procedures, and
compliance details may vary significantly.
ANSI Standards – Practical Use (U.S. Focus)
Although ANSI standards are voluntary, they play a critical role in industry safety:
• OSHA frequently references ANSI standards, making them widely accepted as best practice
• Following ANSI is typically safer and more efficient than developing internal standards from scratch
ANSI Z359 Fall Protection System Includes:
• Z359.1 / Z359.2 – Program management requirements
• Z359.3 – Safety requirements for rescue systems
• Z359.11 – Performance requirements for full-body harnesses
Equipment & Compliance
• All fall protection equipment (e.g., harnesses, lanyards, connectors) must meet ANSI performance requirements
• Manufacturers are responsible for:
12. Testing equipment against ANSI standards
13. Ensuring compliance and proper labeling
Equipment must always be used in accordance with manufacturer instructions and applicable standards.
Key Takeaway
In the United States:
• Follow OSHA regulations
• Use ANSI-compliant equipment
• Always inspect equipment and check tags before use
Understanding and adhering to these standards ensures legal compliance, safety, and best practice in working at
height.

Fall Arrest – ANSI Z359.2
Fall Arrest (ANSI Z359.2)
Fall arrest systems are designed to stop a worker after a fall has occurred, preventing contact with the ground or
lower level.
In fall arrest:
• The worker has already fallen
• The harness and connecting system absorb energy and safely stop the fall
Important Reality
A fall arrest event can be:
• Physically demanding and uncomfortable
• Associated with high forces on the body
• Proper setup is critical to minimize injury
Fall Arrest Attachment Points
There are two primary harness connection points used for fall arrest:
• Sternal (Front Chest D-Ring)
Used for limited fall distances
Lower force limits
• Dorsal (Back D-Ring – between shoulder blades)
Primary point for traditional fall arrest systems
Allows greater fall distance and higher forces
Key Takeaway
Fall arrest = last line of defense
Always:
• Minimize fall distance
• Select the correct attachment point
• Ensure system is properly designed

Fall Arrest – ANSI Z359.2
Fall Arrest Requirements (ANSI Z359.2)
ANSI Z359.2 defines requirements for fall arrest systems, including limits based on connection points:
Sternal (Front) Connection
• Maximum fall distance: 2 ft
• Maximum arrest force (peak): 900 lbs (4 kN)
• Average arrest force: 450 lbs (2 kN)
Dorsal (Back) Connection
• Maximum fall distance: 6 ft
• Maximum arrest force (peak): 1,800 lbs (8 kN)
• Average arrest force: 900 lbs (4 kN)
Key Takeaway
• Sternal connection = lower forces, shorter falls
• Dorsal connection = higher limits, longer allowable fall distance

Work Positioning (ANSI Z359.2)
Work positioning systems are designed to hold a worker in place while preventing access to

In this system:
• The worker is restrained from reaching an edge

Load Angles
Anchor Angles & Load Distribution Simple Rule to Remember
• Smaller angle = Safer system
What is the Included Angle? • Larger angle = Higher force on anchors
The included angle is:
• The angle between two anchor lines (rope-to-rope)
• Measured on the inside of the system Key Takeaway
• Keep angles ≤ 90° whenever possible
How Angle Affects Load • Never approach or exceed 120°
As the included angle increases: Proper anchor angle control is essential for safe
• Force on each anchor increases load distribution and system integrity
• Load sharing becomes less efficient
Key Angle Rules
Preffered Zone
• ≤ 90°
• Best load distribution
• Lower force on each anchor
Critical Zone
• ≈ 120°
• Each anchor carries ~100% of the load
Danger Zone
• > 120°
• Forces increase rapidly and exponentially
• High risk of anchor failure
Why It Matters
• Overload anchor points
• Increase failure risk
• Compromise entire system safety

WLL vs MBS – Understanding Load Limits
Definitions
Minimum Breaking Strength (MBS) Important Reminder
• The maximum load a component can break before failure • Never load equipment near its MBS
• Determined under controlled test conditions • Always operate within WLL limits
• Represents the absolute limit (failure point) • Consider additional forces (shock load, angles,
dynamic movement)
Working Load Limit (WLL)
• The maximum safe load during normal use Key Takeaway
• Based on a safety factor applied to MBS MBS = Breaking point
• Ensures a margin to prevent failure WLL = Safe working limit
Safe systems rely on staying well below failure
General Safety Guidelines limits using proper safety factors
• Solid Metal Components (Carabiners, connectors,
anchor hardware)
WLL ≈ 20% (1/5) of MBS
• Fabric & Mechanical Components
(Ropes, slings, harnesses, descenders, ascenders – e.g., ID, Croll)
WLL ≈ 10% (1/10) of MBS
Quick Comparison
MBS
• Failure load
• Not for actual use
• Safety limit reference
WLL
• Safe working load
• Used in real operations
• Includes safety factor
